umayyad-state-of-c-rdoba.name: Caliphate of Córdoba
umayyad-state-of-c-rdoba.summary: Arab Islamic state ruled by the Umayyad dynasty in Iberia from 756 to 1031, first as an emirate and from 929 as a caliphate, with its capital at Córdoba becoming a centre of trade and learning.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

menahem-ben-saruq.name: Menahem ben Saruq
menahem-ben-saruq.summary: A 10th-century Spanish-Jewish philologist and poet (c. 920–c. 970) who compiled an early Hebrew dictionary and served statesman Hasdai ibn Shaprut.

ahmad-al-maqqari.name: Ahmad al-Maqqari
ahmad-al-maqqari.summary: Algerian scholar, biographer and historian who lived from 1577 to 1632, best known for his Nafh at-Tib, a compendium on the history of Al-Andalus that served as a standard scholarly reference into the twentieth century.

aljarafe.name: Aljarafe
aljarafe.summary: Olive-growing hilly region between Seville and Niebla in Andalusia, along the Guadiamar river.

byzantine-iconoclasm.name: Byzantine Iconoclasm
byzantine-iconoclasm.summary: Two periods (about 726–787 and 814–842) when Byzantine religious and imperial authorities opposed the veneration of icons, causing civil wars and destruction of religious images.

saint-catherine-s-monastery.name: Saint Catherine's Monastery
saint-catherine-s-monastery.summary: Christian monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, Egypt, built 548 to 565 under Byzantine emperor Justinian I; the world's oldest continuously inhabited Christian monastery.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

basilica-of-san-vitale.name: San Vitale in Ravenna
basilica-of-san-vitale.summary: A 6th-century church in Ravenna, Italy, an important surviving example of early Byzantine art, famed for mosaics including a portrait of Emperor Justinian I.

palatine-chapel-aachen.name: Palatine Chapel, Aachen
palatine-chapel-aachen.summary: An early medieval chapel, the surviving core of Charlemagne's palace at Aachen, which later hosted royal coronations from 936 to 1531.

aachen.name: Aachen
aachen.summary: A German city near the Belgian and Dutch borders that became the main royal residence of the Frankish Empire under Charlemagne around 800 CE and the coronation site of 31 Holy Roman Emperors.

san-lorenzo-fuori-le-mura.name: San Lorenzo fuori le Mura
san-lorenzo-fuori-le-mura.summary: One of Rome's five papal basilicas, built as the shrine over the tomb of the martyred deacon Saint Lawrence.

sant-agnese-fuori-le-mura.name: Sant'Agnese fuori le mura
sant-agnese-fuori-le-mura.summary: A basilica in Rome built above the catacombs where Saint Agnes was buried, constructed by Pope Honorius I in the 7th century and noted for its well-preserved apse mosaic.

santo-stefano-al-monte-celio.name: Santo Stefano Rotondo
santo-stefano-al-monte-celio.summary: An ancient round basilica on Rome's Caelian Hill dedicated to the first Christian martyr Stephen and to Hungary's first king, also named Stephen.

archbasilica-of-saint-john-lateran.name: Lateran Basilica
archbasilica-of-saint-john-lateran.summary: The Catholic cathedral of Rome and seat of the pope, founded in 324 and considered the oldest public church and basilica in the Western world.

pope-john-vii.name: Pope John VII
pope-john-vii.summary: Bishop of Rome from 705 to 707, an ethnic Greek pope who got along better with the Lombards ruling Italy than with the Byzantine emperor.

old-st-peter-s-basilica.name: Old St. Peter's Basilica
old-st-peter-s-basilica.summary: The original basilica that stood in Vatican City from the 4th to 16th centuries, built under Roman Emperor Constantine I on the site of today's St. Peter's Basilica.

orans.name: Orans posture
orans.summary: A standing prayer posture with arms raised and palms up, common in early Christian art and still used in some Eastern Christian liturgies today.

belisarius.name: Belisarius
belisarius.summary: A Byzantine military commander (c. 500-565) under Emperor Justinian I who reconquered North Africa and much of Italy, considered one of history's greatest generals.

narses.name: Narses
narses.summary: A Roman general and statesman of Armenian heritage (c. 478–573) who helped reconquer Italy for Emperor Justinian I, defeating the Ostrogoths at Taginae in 552 and Mons Lactarius in 553.

ostrogothic-kingdom.name: Ostrogothic Kingdom
ostrogothic-kingdom.summary: A Germanic kingdom ruling Italy from 493 to 553, founded by Theodoric the Great after he killed the previous ruler Odoacer; at its height it reached from southern France to western Serbia.

gothic-war-535-554.name: Gothic War (535–554)
gothic-war-535-554.summary: A war from 535 to 554 in which the Byzantine Empire fought the Ostrogoths for control of Italy, leaving the peninsula devastated and depopulated.

umayyad-caliphate.name: Umayyad Caliphate
umayyad-caliphate.summary: Second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 661 to 750 from its capital Damascus; expanded Muslim rule across the Maghreb, Iberia, Central Asia and Sindh.

roderic.name: King Roderic
roderic.summary: Visigothic king of Hispania from 710 to 711, the last Goth to rule from Toledo, defeated and killed by Umayyad invaders at the Battle of Guadalete.

visigothic-kingdom.name: Visigothic Kingdom
visigothic-kingdom.summary: Germanic kingdom that ruled southwestern France and most of the Iberian Peninsula from the 5th to the 8th century, one of the successor states to the Western Roman Empire.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.name: Kingdom of the Lombards
kingdom-of-the-lombards.summary: An early medieval state founded by the Germanic Lombards in Italy in the late 500s CE, ruled from Pavia, that opposed the Byzantine Empire until Charlemagne conquered it in 774.

duchy-of-rome.name: Duchy of Rome
duchy-of-rome.summary: A Byzantine-ruled state within the Exarchate of Ravenna, often at odds with the Papacy, which ceased to function as an administrative unit after the Papal States formed in 756.

totila.name: Totila
totila.summary: The penultimate King of the Ostrogoths (died 552), who reversed the Gothic War's tide and recaptured Rome from Belisarius in 546.

teia.name: Teia
teia.summary: Last king of the Ostrogoths, killed in 552; he served as Totila's second-in-command in the Gothic War and led the final Gothic resistance against Byzantium before his death ended the kingdom.

battle-of-taginae.name: Battle of Taginae
battle-of-taginae.summary: A battle fought in July 552 in which Byzantine forces under Narses defeated the Ostrogoths under King Totila, paving the way for the Byzantine reconquest of Italy and the end of the Gothic Kingdom.

battle-of-mons-lactarius.name: Battle of Mons Lactarius
battle-of-mons-lactarius.summary: An October 552 battle near Mount Vesuvius in which Byzantine forces under Narses defeated the Ostrogoths and killed their king Teia, ending the Gothic state in Italy.

pope-leo-iv.name: Pope Leo IV
pope-leo-iv.summary: Bishop of Rome and leader of the Papal States from 847 to 855, remembered for repairing churches damaged in an Arab raid and building the Leonine Wall around Vatican Hill.

leonine-city.name: Leonine Walls
leonine-city.summary: A defensive wall built around the Vatican district of Rome on the orders of Pope Leo IV in the 9th century, protecting the area that held St Peter's Basilica; the enclosed district became known as the Leonine City.

exarchate-of-ravenna.name: Exarchate of Ravenna
exarchate-of-ravenna.summary: The Byzantine Empire's administrative district in Italy, governed from Ravenna by an exarch from around 584 until most of its territory fell to the Lombards in 751.

duchy-of-naples.name: Duchy of Naples
duchy-of-naples.summary: A Byzantine province that became a de facto independent state centered on Naples, lasting over five centuries through the Early and High Middle Ages under a military governor.

muslim-conquest-of-the-iberian-peninsula.name: Umayyad conquest of Hispania
muslim-conquest-of-the-iberian-peninsula.summary: Conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula by the Umayyad Caliphate in the early 8th century, ending Christian rule and establishing Muslim al-Andalus.
muslim-conquest-of-the-iberian-peninsula.source_title: Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

kingdom-of-asturias.name: Kingdom of Asturias
kingdom-of-asturias.summary: The first Christian kingdom established in the Iberian Peninsula after the Umayyad conquest, founded by Pelagius following his 722 victory at Covadonga, seen as the start of the Reconquista.

reconquista.name: Reconquista
reconquista.summary: A centuries-long series of military campaigns by Christian kingdoms in Iberia against Muslim-ruled al-Andalus, beginning around 718 to 722 and ending in 1492 with the capture of Granada.

tariq-ibn-ziyad.name: Tariq ibn Ziyad
tariq-ibn-ziyad.summary: Umayyad commander (c. 670 – c. 720) who initiated the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula, crossing from North Africa to defeat the Visigothic Kingdom between 711 and 718.

tangier.name: Tangier
tangier.summary: City in northwestern Morocco on the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, a Phoenician trading hub turned international zone in 1923 until Moroccan independence.

tarif-ibn-malik.name: Tarif ibn Malik
tarif-ibn-malik.summary: A Berber commander under Tariq ibn Ziyad who led a reconnaissance raid into Iberia in 710 CE, paving the way for the conquest of Visigothic Hispania.

procopius.name: Procopius
procopius.summary: A Greek historian from Caesarea, about 500 to 565, who accompanied the Byzantine general Belisarius and became the principal historian of Emperor Justinian's era.

rugii.name: Rugii
rugii.summary: A small Germanic people first recorded near the Baltic in the 1st century who later formed a short-lived 5th-century kingdom on the Danube before being absorbed into the Ostrogothic Kingdom.

alemanni.name: Alemanni
alemanni.summary: A confederation of Germanic peoples that emerged east of the Upper Rhine in the 3rd century AD, later seizing Roman land and giving rise to the region called Alamannia.

battle-of-the-volturnus.name: Battle of the Volturnus
battle-of-the-volturnus.summary: A 554 CE battle near Italy's Volturno River in which Byzantine general Narses defeated an invading force of Franks and Alemanni, ending the Gothic War.

duchy-of-benevento.name: Duchy of Benevento
duchy-of-benevento.summary: The southernmost Lombard duchy in Italy, centered on Benevento from 571 to 774, which survived as an independent principality for nearly 300 years after the Lombard kingdom's fall.

principality-of-benevento.name: Principality of Benevento
principality-of-benevento.summary: The sole Lombard territory to survive as an independent state after the Franks conquered the Kingdom of the Lombards, until the Norman Robert Guiscard captured it in 1053.

otto-the-great.name: Otto the Great
otto-the-great.summary: East Frankish king from 936 and Holy Roman Emperor from 962 to 973, who unified the German duchies, defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955, and was crowned emperor by Pope John XII.

adelaide-of-italy.name: Adelaide of Italy
adelaide-of-italy.summary: Holy Roman Empress (931–999) by marriage to Otto the Great, crowned in Rome in 962; later regent of the empire for her grandson from 991 to 995, and a model for future royal consorts.

kingdom-of-italy-holy-roman-empire.name: Kingdom of Italy (Holy Roman Empire)
kingdom-of-italy-holy-roman-empire.summary: A constituent kingdom of the Holy Roman Empire covering northern and central Italy, ruled from Pavia, whose crown Otto I of Germany seized in 951 before his imperial coronation in 962.

pavia.name: Pavia
pavia.summary: A town in Lombardy, Northern Italy, that served as capital of the Ostrogothic Kingdom, then the Kingdom of the Lombards, then the Kingdom of Italy across the medieval period.

aghlabid-dynasty.name: Aghlabid dynasty
aghlabid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya from 800 to 909 as nominal Abbasid vassals, also conquering Sicily and parts of southern Italy, before falling to the Fatimids.

kalbids.name: Kalbids
kalbids.summary: A Muslim Arab dynasty that ruled the Emirate of Sicily from 948 to 1053, initially appointed by the Fatimids before gaining effective autonomy.

boethius.name: Boethius
boethius.summary: Roman senator, consul and philosopher (c. 480–524 CE) who translated Greek classics into Latin, becoming a central bridge between Classical and Christian scholarship.

on-the-consolation-of-philosophy.name: The Consolation of Philosophy
on-the-consolation-of-philosophy.summary: Philosophical work written by Boethius in 523 while imprisoned and awaiting execution, often called the last great Western work of the Classical Period.

theodoric-the-great.name: Theodoric the Great
theodoric-the-great.summary: King of the Ostrogoths (471–526) who ruled Italy and controlled a realm stretching from the Atlantic to the Adriatic, exercising imperial powers recognized by Constantinople.

hugh-fraser-stewart.name: Hugh Fraser Stewart
hugh-fraser-stewart.summary: British academic, churchman and literary critic (1863–1948).

isidore-of-seville.name: Isidore of Seville
isidore-of-seville.summary: A Hispano-Roman scholar and archbishop of Seville (c. 560–636) who helped convert Visigothic kings to Catholicism and wrote the Etymologiae, an influential encyclopedia preserving classical knowledge.

etymologiae.name: Etymologiae
etymologiae.summary: An etymological encyclopedia compiled by the bishop Isidore of Seville toward the end of his life, summarizing knowledge from hundreds of classical sources; it became a widely used medieval textbook.

braulio-of-zaragoza.name: Braulio of Zaragoza
braulio-of-zaragoza.summary: Bishop of Zaragoza (c. 585–651 AD) and a learned cleric of the Visigothic Kingdom, celebrated as one of its most notable saints.

menippean-satire.name: Menippean satire
menippean-satire.summary: A form of prose satire that mocks mental attitudes and social types rather than specific people, mixing allegory, parody and shifting styles and viewpoints.

nicomachus.name: Nicomachus
nicomachus.summary: Greek Neopythagorean philosopher (c. 60–120 AD) whose writings on arithmetic and music became standard textbooks into the medieval period.

porphyry-of-tyre.name: Porphyry
porphyry-of-tyre.summary: A Phoenician Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305) who edited his teacher Plotinus's works and wrote an introduction to logic used throughout the Middle Ages.

cassiodorus.name: Cassiodorus
cassiodorus.summary: Roman statesman and scholar (c. 485–c. 585) who served Theodoric the Great before founding the Vivarium monastery and devoting himself to Christian learning.

vivarium-monastery.name: Vivarium monastery
vivarium-monastery.summary: Monastery founded around 544 by the Roman statesman Cassiodorus in Calabria, Italy, with a library and study center that preserved Greek and Latin classical literature.

ibn-wahshiyya.name: Ibn Wahshiyya
ibn-wahshiyya.summary: An Iraqi Aramaic-speaking agriculturalist, toxicologist and alchemist who died around 930, best known for his influential Arabic work on agriculture, astrology and magic.

the-nabataean-agriculture.name: The Nabataean Agriculture
the-nabataean-agriculture.summary: A 10th-century Arabic text on agronomy by Ibn Wahshiyya, the first and most influential Arabic book on the subject, its influence spreading from Yemen to Spain.

al-zahrawi.name: Al-Zahrawi
al-zahrawi.summary: An Arab physician and surgeon from al-Andalus (c. 936–1013), considered one of the greatest surgeons of the Middle Ages and author of a 30-volume medical encyclopedia.

magister-officiorum.name: Magister officiorum
magister-officiorum.summary: One of the most senior administrative offices in the Later Roman and early Byzantine Empire, later reduced to an honorary rank until it disappeared in the 12th century.

t-and-o-map.name: T and O map
t-and-o-map.summary: An early type of world map, also called an Isidoran map, showing the known landmass as a circle divided into three parts by a T-shaped arrangement of the Mediterranean, the river Tanais and the Nile.

beatus-of-li-bana.name: Beatus of Liébana
beatus-of-li-bana.summary: Monk, theologian and author, around 730 to after 785, whose Commentary on the Apocalypse survives in 27 illustrated manuscripts prized as outstanding works of Mozarabic art, though little else is known of his life.

paul-the-deacon.name: Paul the Deacon
paul-the-deacon.summary: Benedictine monk, scribe and historian of the Lombards, active in the 8th century.

origo-gentis-langobardorum.name: Origo Gentis Langobardorum
origo-gentis-langobardorum.summary: A short 7th-century Latin text giving a founding myth and early king-list of the Lombard people, used as a source by later chroniclers.

liber-pontificalis.name: Liber Pontificalis
liber-pontificalis.summary: A collection of papal biographies from Saint Peter to the 15th century, quoted almost uncritically as a historical source from the 8th to 18th centuries.

secundus-of-trent.name: Secundus of Trent
secundus-of-trent.summary: A late 6th and early 7th-century deacon, later abbot, who served the archbishop of Ravenna and the Lombard king Agilulf's court, and wrote a history of the Lombards up to 612.

bede.name: Bede
bede.summary: An English Benedictine monk (672/3-735) called the 'Father of English History' for his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, and a noted scholar of scripture and calendars.

neume.name: Neumes
neume.summary: A basic symbol of early Western musical notation used before five-line staff notation, showing the shape of a melody and later relative pitch.

pembroke-college-cambridge.name: Pembroke College, Cambridge
pembroke-college-cambridge.summary: A constituent college of the University of Cambridge, the third-oldest there, with buildings from nearly every century since its founding and a strong academic record.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

natural-history-pliny.name: Natural History
natural-history-pliny.summary: Encyclopedic Latin work by Pliny the Elder, published around AD 77, the largest surviving single work from the Roman Empire, covering topics from astronomy to art and precious stones.

abbas-ibn-firnas.name: Abbas ibn Firnas
abbas-ibn-firnas.summary: Andalusi polymath, c. 809-887, who experimented with unpowered flight and made contributions in astronomy, engineering and glassmaking.

reading-stone.name: Reading stone
reading-stone.summary: An early magnifying lens placed over text to aid reading, credited to Abbas ibn Firnas in the 9th century and used before spectacles emerged in the late 13th century.

schola-medica-salernitana.name: Schola Medica Salernitana
schola-medica-salernitana.summary: Medieval medical school in Salerno, Italy, founded in the 9th century and the leading source of medical knowledge in Western Europe by the 10th, blending Greek and Arabic traditions.

monte-cassino.name: Monte Cassino
monte-cassino.summary: A Benedictine abbey near Rome, founded around 529 by Benedict of Nursia as the order's first monastery, repeatedly sacked and rebuilt over the centuries.

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 460–370 BC) traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine' for pioneering prognosis and clinical observation, and credited with the Hippocratic Oath.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

dioscorides.name: Dioscorides
dioscorides.summary: Greek physician and botanist (c. 40-90 AD) called the 'father of pharmacognosy', who wrote De materia medica, a five-volume encyclopedia on herbal medicine read for over 1,500 years.

maslama-al-majriti.name: Maslama al-Majriti
maslama-al-majriti.summary: A Muslim Arab astronomer, mathematician, and alchemist active in al-Andalus around 950 to 1007, during the reign of Al-Hakam II.

al-hakam-ii.name: Al-Hakam II
al-hakam-ii.summary: Caliph of Córdoba from 961 to 976, the second Umayyad Caliph of Córdoba in Al-Andalus and son of Abd al-Rahman III.

said-al-andalusi.name: Said al-Andalusi
said-al-andalusi.summary: An Arab judge of Toledo in al-Andalus (1029-1070) who wrote on the history of science and philosophy, and compiled a famous biographical encyclopedia of scientists.

ibn-as-saffar.name: Ibn as-Saffar
ibn-as-saffar.summary: A Spanish-Arab astronomer in Al-Andalus who died in 1035, best known for a treatise on the astrolabe that stayed in use until the 15th century and influenced Kepler.

abbey-of-saint-gall.name: Abbey of Saint Gall
abbey-of-saint-gall.summary: A Benedictine monastery in Switzerland founded in 719, later an independent principality and home to one of the world's oldest monastic libraries.

muhammad-i-of-c-rdoba.name: Muhammad I of Córdoba
muhammad-i-of-c-rdoba.summary: The fifth Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus, who lived from 823 to 886, during a period of thriving art, architecture and culture that made Córdoba a cultural and political center.

beatus-map.name: Beatus map
beatus-map.summary: An influential early medieval world map based on the work of monk Beatus of Liébana, meant to illustrate the biblical dispersion of the Apostles rather than exact geography.

zij-as-sindhind.name: Sindhind
zij-as-sindhind.summary: An 8th-century Arabic astronomical work brought to Baghdad from India and translated for Caliph al-Mansur, based on Brahmagupta's Sanskrit treatise.

lombards.name: Lombards
lombards.summary: A Germanic people who conquered most of the Italian Peninsula between 568 and 774 AD, giving their name to the region of Lombardy.

arianism.name: Arianism
arianism.summary: A Christian doctrine, named after the priest Arius, teaching that Jesus was created by God rather than co-eternal with him; later regarded as heretical by mainstream Christianity.

reccared-i.name: Reccared I
reccared-i.summary: King of the Visigoths who ruled from 586 to 601, marking a major shift by renouncing Arianism in favor of Chalcedonian Christianity in 587.

pope-leo-iii.name: Pope Leo III
pope-leo-iii.summary: Bishop of Rome and leader of the Papal States from 795 to 816, protected by Charlemagne and famous for crowning him emperor.

list-of-kings-of-the-lombards.name: King of the Lombards
list-of-kings-of-the-lombards.summary: Title held by monarchs of the Lombard people from the early 6th century; after 774 it passed to Frankish rulers, including Charlemagne.
list-of-kings-of-the-lombards.source_title: List of kings of the Lombards

pepin-of-italy.name: Pepin of Italy
pepin-of-italy.summary: King of Italy from 781 to 810, third son of Charlemagne, crowned king of the Lombard Kingdom at his baptism; his son Bernard succeeded him.

king-of-italy.name: King of Italy
king-of-italy.summary: A title held by rulers of Italy after Rome's fall, used by Odoacer, Ostrogothic kings, Carolingian and Holy Roman emperors, and later by Napoleon and Italy's House of Savoy until 1946.

louis-the-pious.name: Louis the Pious
louis-the-pious.summary: King of the Franks and co-emperor with his father Charlemagne from 813, sole ruler after 814, who conquered Barcelona and divided the empire among his sons.

lothair-i.name: Lothair I
lothair-i.summary: 9th-century Carolingian emperor (817–855) and king of Italy and Middle Francia, whose wars with his brothers after their father's death split Charlemagne's empire.

middle-francia.name: Middle Francia
middle-francia.summary: A short-lived Frankish kingdom created in 843 by the Treaty of Verdun for Lothair I, split among his sons in 855 and later absorbed by West and East Francia.

treaty-of-pr-m.name: Treaty of Prüm
treaty-of-pr-m.summary: 855 agreement dividing Emperor Lothair I's realm of Middle Francia among his three sons as he approached death.

louis-ii-of-italy.name: Louis II of Italy
louis-ii-of-italy.summary: King of Italy and Carolingian emperor from 844 (ruling alone after 855), who took the title emperor of the Romans after conquering Bari in 871.

spoleto.name: Spoleto
spoleto.summary: An ancient city in central Italy that became a Roman colony in 241 BC and later the seat of the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto from 576.

charles-the-fat.name: Charles the Fat
charles-the-fat.summary: Carolingian emperor from 881 to 887 and great-grandson of Charlemagne; the last legitimate Carolingian to rule a reunited Frankish empire, he was deposed in a coup in 887.

duchy-of-amalfi.name: Duchy of Amalfi
duchy-of-amalfi.summary: A largely independent Italian state centered on Amalfi in the 10th and 11th centuries, whose merchants once dominated Mediterranean trade before it fell to Norman conquest in 1073.

gaeta.name: Gaeta
gaeta.summary: Seaside city in Lazio, Italy, with walls dating to Roman times, historically one of the nominally Byzantine early medieval Italian city-states.

plato.name: Plato
plato.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 428–347 BC) considered the foundational thinker of Western philosophy, who founded the Academy in Athens and developed the Theory of Forms.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

third-council-of-toledo.name: Third Council of Toledo
third-council-of-toledo.summary: Church council of 589 that marked Visigothic Spain's entry into the Catholic Church. It also enacted restrictions on Jews, and the conversion led to repeated conflict with them.

filioque.name: Filioque
filioque.summary: Latin for "and the Son", a clause in the Nicene Creed about whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or also from the Son. It is a major cause of the 1054 split between Western and Eastern churches.

peter-of-pisa.name: Peter of Pisa
peter-of-pisa.summary: Italian grammarian, deacon and poet (744–799) summoned to Charlemagne's court in 776, where he served as the emperor's primary Latin teacher.

alcuin.name: Alcuin of York
alcuin.summary: Anglo-Saxon scholar and teacher (c. 735–804) from York who led Charlemagne's court school and helped shape the Carolingian Renaissance.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

cicero.name: Cicero
cicero.summary: A Roman statesman, lawyer, philosopher and orator (106–43 BC) who served as consul in 63 BC and greatly shaped the Latin language through his surviving writings.

visigoths.name: Visigoths
visigoths.summary: Gothic people who sacked Rome in 410 under Alaric I and later ruled a kingdom spanning southern Gaul and then Iberia for two centuries, until its fall in 711.

migration-period.name: Migration Period
migration-period.summary: A period from about 300 to 600 CE of large-scale movements of peoples into Europe that contributed to the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

benedictines.name: Benedictines
benedictines.summary: A Catholic monastic order founded in 529 by Benedict of Nursia, the oldest religious order in the Latin Church, organized as autonomous monasteries rather than one hierarchy.

carolingian-empire.name: Carolingian Empire
carolingian-empire.summary: A Frankish-led empire in Western and Central Europe from 800 to 887, begun when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor; it later split into separate kingdoms.

santa-prassede.name: Santa Prassede
santa-prassede.summary: An early medieval basilica in Rome dedicated to the second-century Saint Praxedes, served by Benedictine monks since 1198.

santa-cecilia-in-trastevere.name: Santa Cecilia in Trastevere
santa-cecilia-in-trastevere.summary: A basilica in Rome's Trastevere district dedicated to Saint Cecilia, patron saint of music, rebuilt in the 9th century and known for its mosaics and her relics.

santi-nereo-e-achilleo.name: Santi Nereo e Achilleo
santi-nereo-e-achilleo.summary: A fourth-century basilica church in Rome, near the Baths of Caracalla, dedicated to the martyrs Nereo and Achilleo and still a working titular cardinal church.

santa-maria-in-domnica.name: Santa Maria in Domnica
santa-maria-in-domnica.summary: A Roman Catholic basilica in Rome dedicated to the Virgin Mary, considered one of the finest examples of the Carolingian Renaissance in the city.
